newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian, Ukraine leaders meet amid fleet row.
newsitem.headline: Russian, Ukraine leaders meet amid fleet row.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma met ailing Russian leader Boris Yeltsin on Thursday for talks overshadowed by a row on dividing the Black Sea fleet.
Just before Kuchma arrived, Russia's lower house of parliament warned Ukraine that Moscow would never give up control of the Crimean port of Sevastopol, home to the disputed fleet.
The State Duma issued the warning in an appeal a day after deputies voted overwhelmingly to freeze division between Russia and Ukraine of the 600-vessel fleet.

"It is not just presidents and prime ministers who suffer from the lack of understanding between Russia and Ukraine in some areas, but the people of both countries as well," Interfax news agency quoted Kuchma as saying on arrival.

"There are questions, they have to be solved, and let there be goodwill on both sides," he said before setting off for the Barvikha sanatorium outside Moscow where Yeltsin is preparing for heart surgery next month.
Russia and Ukraine have wrangled off and on since the Soviet Union split up in December 1991 over what to do with the ageing Black Sea fleet.

Broad accords have already been signed dividing the fleet but no decision has been reached on a share-out of bases and on Sevastopol which the Duma said still fell under Russian jurisdiction although Crimea is part of Ukraine.

"Sevastopol was, is and will be the main naval base of Russia's Black Sea fleet. Unilateral moves by Ukraine to divide it will lead not just to the division but the destruction of the Black Sea fleet -- the Duma thinks the division of the fleet has to be stopped," read the appeal.

The Duma said a Soviet decree of 1948 which put Sevastopol under Moscow's direct rule was still valid and that Russia, as the successor state to the Soviet Union, therefore still had jurisdiction over the port.
Yeltsin's representative in the Duma made clear that Wednesday's vote had not been coordinated with the president.
Parliamentary analysts say there is little chance Yeltsin would back the move, which is likely to upset already uneasy relations between the two Slav former Soviet states.
Kuchma reacted angrily, saying the vote could lead to "a worsening in relations between the Ukrainian and Russian people," and not just between two legislatures.
He said a firm deal had been reached on Tuesday by members of a joint commission which foresaw Moscow paying rent to keep ships at the Crimean port of Sevastopol, in Ukraine.
But Russia's Itar-Tass news agency quoted a source in Yeltsin's administration as saying the Russian leader did not share such optimism.

Kuchma said the two countries were closer than ever to signing a major political treaty on future realations, but that he had come to Moscow mainly to find out how Yeltsin was feeling before heart surgery planned for next month.
"(The meeting) will not comprise deep discussions of all the problems affecting relations between Ukraine and Russia. I just want to have a chat with Boris Nikolayevich (Yeltsin)," he said.
Before falling ill in June, Yeltsin had postponed six trips to Kiev to sign a friendship treaty in 20 months.
